learn.hook: Stretch a rubber band and it snaps back; squeeze a lump of atta dough and it stays squashed. Same push, very different materials.
points: A rigid body is only an idealisation: every real body deforms (changes shape or size) when forces act on it.
Elasticity: the property of a body to regain its original size and shape when the deforming force is removed.
Plasticity: the body does not regain its shape and is permanently deformed.
Elastic examples: steel, rubber (within limits); nearly plastic examples: putty, wet clay, mud, dough.
Engineers must know elastic behaviour to design bridges, buildings, cranes, machines and even artificial body parts.

example.q: A steel spring is stretched slightly and released; a clay ball is pressed and released. Classify each behaviour.
steps: The spring returns to its original length: elastic.
The clay keeps its new dented shape: plastic.
So steel (within limits) is elastic and clay is plastic.

learn.reallife: The pottery artisans of Khurja rely on the plasticity of wet clay to shape cups and vases on the wheel.

learn.hook: A heavy train crossing the Chenab rail bridge sets up stresses inside every steel member. Engineers calculate each one.
points: When a body is deformed, internal restoring forces appear. Stress = restoring force per unit area = F/A. SI unit N m⁻² = pascal (Pa).
Longitudinal stress: force normal to the cross-section. Tensile stress when stretched, compressive stress when compressed.
Shearing (tangential) stress: force parallel to the surface (e.g. pushing the top of a book sideways).
Hydraulic (volume) stress: equal force per unit area on all sides (e.g. a body deep in water); it equals the pressure.

example.q: A steel rod of cross-section 2 × 10⁻⁴ m² supports a load of 4 × 10⁴ N. Find the stress.
steps: Stress = F/A.
= 2 × 10⁸ Pa (tensile).

learn.hook: Hang a 1 kg mass on a 1 m steel wire and it stretches less than a hair's width. Strain measures that tiny change as a fraction.
points: Strain = fractional change in size or shape. Longitudinal strain = ΔL/L; shearing strain = Δx/L = tan θ ≈ θ; volume strain = ΔV/V.
Strain is a ratio of like quantities, so it has no units or dimensions.
Hooke's law: for small deformations, stress ∝ strain, i.e. stress = k × strain.
The proportionality constant k is the modulus of elasticity (Young's, shear or bulk modulus, depending on the type of stress).
Hooke's law is an empirical law and holds only within the elastic (proportional) limit.

example.q: A 2 m wire stretches by 1 mm under a load. Find the longitudinal strain.
steps: Strain = ΔL/L.
= 5 × 10⁻⁴ (no units).

learn.hook: Testing labs pull a steel rod until it snaps, plotting stress against strain. That curve tells engineers everything about the metal.
points: For a metal under tension, the curve starts as a straight line (O to A): Hooke's law holds up to the proportional limit.
Beyond A, up to the yield point (elastic limit) B, the body still returns to its shape but stress is no longer proportional to strain. The stress at B is the yield strength σ_y.
Beyond B is the plastic region: if the load is removed (say at C), the body does not return; the remaining strain is the permanent set.
Stress rises to a maximum, the ultimate tensile strength σ_u (point D); beyond it, the wire thins locally and breaks at the fracture point E, even with less stress.

example.q: On a stress–strain curve, a wire is loaded to point C beyond the yield point and unloaded. What happens?
steps: C lies in the plastic region.
When unloaded, the curve comes down roughly parallel to OA but does not reach O.
The wire keeps a permanent strain called the permanent set.

learn.reallife: Steel plants grade TMT bars for Indian construction by their yield strength, e.g. 'Fe 500' means a yield strength of about 500 MPa.

games.title: Curve facts
items: Hooke's law holds up to the proportional limit.
Beyond the yield point, the wire returns fully to its original length when unloaded.
The ultimate tensile strength is the maximum stress the material can withstand.
Fracture can occur at a stress lower than the ultimate tensile strength.
After necking, stress falls before fracture.

It is the stress at the yield point.

teach.ask: Gappu watched a lab video of a steel rod being pulled till it snapped. Explain the stress–strain curve and its key points.

revise.summary: A metal's stress–strain curve is straight up to the proportional limit, still elastic up to the yield point (yield strength σ_y), then plastic. It peaks at the ultimate tensile strength σ_u and breaks at the fracture point; unloading in the plastic region leaves a permanent set.
focus: Label the regions and points of the stress–strain curve
Define yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and permanent set
Explain what happens on unloading beyond the yield point
remember: O–A: Hooke's law (proportional limit A)
A–B: elastic but not linear; B = yield point, stress σ_y

learn.hook: Copper can be drawn into thin wires; a glass rod just snaps. The stress–strain curve explains why.
points: Ductile materials (copper, aluminium, mild steel) have a large plastic region between the ultimate tensile strength and fracture; they can be drawn into wires.
Brittle materials (glass, cast iron, ceramics) fracture soon after the ultimate tensile strength is reached, with little plastic flow.
Elastomers (rubber, the tissue of the aorta) can be stretched to large strains and still return; their curve has no well-defined linear (Hooke's law) region.
Steel has a much larger Young's modulus than rubber, so for the same stress it strains far less. In the physics sense, steel is MORE elastic than rubber.

example.q: Two wires of the same size, one of steel (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) and one of copper (Y = 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa), carry equal loads. Which stretches more?
steps: ΔL = FL/(AY), so ΔL ∝ 1/Y for the same F, L, A.
Copper has the smaller Y.
Copper stretches more (about 2/1.1 ≈ 1.8 times steel).

learn.reallife: Electricians in India prefer copper wiring partly because copper is ductile: it bends without cracking during installation.

learn.hook: The steel cables of a lift at a Mumbai high-rise stretch a few millimetres every time people step in. Young's modulus predicts exactly how much.
points: Young's modulus Y = longitudinal stress/longitudinal strain = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL). Unit N m⁻² (Pa).
Elongation: ΔL = FL/(AY). Thicker, shorter, stiffer wires stretch less.
Typical values: steel about 2 × 10¹¹ Pa; copper about 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa; aluminium about 7 × 10¹⁰ Pa. (B and G values are also tabulated for materials.)
Two wires joined end to end carrying a load: both have the same tension F. Stress in each = F/A for that wire; elongations add up.

example.q: A 2 m steel wire (A = 10⁻⁶ m², Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) holds a 100 N load. Find the elongation.

Answer: The same
quiz.mistake: Thinks the stiffer wire carries more force

quiz.q: In the joined wires, which one has the greater elongation?
options: Copper, since its Young's modulus is smaller
quiz.explain: Same F, L, A: ΔL ∝ 1/Y.
steps: Same F, L and A: ΔL = FL/(AY) ∝ 1/Y.
Y_copper < Y_steel.
So copper has the greater elongation.
Answer: Copper, since its Young's modulus is smaller

quiz.q: A wire under stress 2 × 10⁸ Pa shows strain 10⁻³. Its Young's modulus in units of 10¹¹ Pa is
quiz.explain: Y = stress/strain = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa.
steps: Y = stress/strain
In units of 10¹¹ Pa: 2
Answer: 2

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A thicker wire of the same material and length stretches less under the same load.
Reason (R): Elongation ΔL = FL/(AY) is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Larger A means smaller stress and hence smaller strain. R explains A.
steps: R: ΔL = FL/(AY), so ΔL ∝ 1/A: true.
A thicker wire has larger A, so it stretches less: A true.
R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

teach.ask: Gappu hung a stone from a thin copper wire and a thick steel wire. Explain Young's modulus and how to predict which stretches more.
teach.praise: ΔL = FL/(AY): thin, long wires of low-Y material stretch the most!
teach.nudge: What is Young's modulus? Which factors make a wire stretch more?

revise.summary: Young's modulus is Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL), a property of the material, so elongation is ΔL = FL/(AY). Thicker, shorter or stiffer wires stretch less, and wires joined in series carry the same tension.
focus: Calculate elongation and Young's modulus
Compare elongations using ΔL ∝ L/(r²Y)
Solve problems with two wires joined end to end
remember: Y = FL/(AΔL); ΔL = FL/(AY)
Steel ≈ 2 × 10¹¹ Pa; copper ≈ 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa; aluminium ≈ 7 × 10¹⁰ Pa
Wires in series carry the same tension
traps: Y depends only on the material, not on load, length or area
Doubling the radius makes the area 4 times, not 2 times

learn.hook: At the deepest point of the Indian Ocean, water is under over 700 atmospheres of pressure, yet its volume shrinks by only about 3%.
points: Shear (rigidity) modulus G = shearing stress/shearing strain = (F/A)/(Δx/L) = FL/(AΔx). For most materials G ≈ Y/3.
Shear displacement of a slab: Δx = FL/(AG).
Bulk modulus B = −p/(ΔV/V) (the minus sign makes B positive, since volume decreases when pressure increases). Compressibility k = 1/B.
Solids have the largest B, liquids smaller, gases the smallest: gases are the most compressible.
Water has B ≈ 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa; glass about 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Pa.

example.q: Water (B = 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa) is subjected to an extra pressure of 2.2 × 10⁷ Pa. Find the fractional decrease in volume.
steps: ΔV/V = −p/B.
= −10⁻², i.e. a 1% decrease.

learn.reallife: Submarines of the Indian Navy are built to withstand enormous hydraulic stress; their hulls use materials with high bulk modulus.

games.title: Bulk modulus: highest to lowest group

quiz.q: A 2 × 10⁵ Pa extra pressure acts on a liquid with B = 2 × 10⁹ Pa. The fractional decrease in volume in units of 10⁻⁴ is
quiz.explain: ΔV/V = p/B = 10⁻⁴.
steps: ΔV/V = p/B
In units of 10⁻⁴: 1
Answer: 1

quiz.q: Compressibility is
quiz.explain: k = 1/B: easy to compress means small B, large k.
steps: Compressibility measures how easily volume changes.
It is defined as k = 1/B.
So it is the reciprocal of bulk modulus.
Answer: The reciprocal of bulk modulus

quiz.q: Which state of matter has the smallest bulk modulus?
quiz.explain: Gases are the most compressible.
steps: Gases are the easiest to compress.
Easy to compress = small bulk modulus.
So gas has the smallest B.
Answer: Gas

quiz.q: A slab with top face 0.01 m² and height 0.1 m (G = 10⁹ Pa) has a tangential force of 1000 N on top. The shear displacement in units of 10⁻⁵ m is
steps: Δx = FL/(AG)
In units of 10⁻⁵ m: 1
Answer: 1

quiz.q: For most materials, the shear modulus G is about
quiz.explain: Empirically G ≈ Y/3.
steps: Shear modulus G = shearing stress/shearing strain.
For most materials, experiment gives G ≈ Y/3.
Answer: Y/3

quiz.q: The minus sign in B = −p/(ΔV/V) is there because
options: An increase in pressure produces a decrease in volume
quiz.explain: ΔV is negative when p increases, so the minus makes B positive.
steps: Increasing pressure makes ΔV negative.
So ΔV/V is negative; the minus sign makes B positive.
The reason: more pressure gives less volume.
Answer: An increase in pressure produces a decrease in volume

quiz.q: A glass slab (B = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Pa) is put under 3.7 × 10⁷ Pa extra pressure. The fractional volume change in units of 10⁻³ is
steps: ΔV/V = p/B
In units of 10⁻³: 1
Answer: 1

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Gases are much more compressible than solids.
Reason (R): The bulk modulus of a gas is larger than that of a solid.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: gases have much smaller bulk moduli, which is why they compress easily.
steps: A: gases compress far more easily than solids: true.
Easy compression means small B, so gases have smaller B than solids: R false.
A is true but R is false.
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Mixes up bulk modulus and compressibility

teach.ask: Gappu pushes the top of a rubber eraser sideways and squeezes a balloon underwater. Explain shear modulus and bulk modulus.
teach.praise: Shear changes shape, bulk changes volume. Gases have tiny B, so they squash the easiest!
teach.nudge: What does shear modulus measure? What does bulk modulus measure? Which state is easiest to compress?

revise.summary: Shear modulus G = (F/A)/(Δx/L), about Y/3 for most materials, and bulk modulus B = −p/(ΔV/V), whose reciprocal is compressibility. Solids have the largest B and gases the smallest, so gases are most compressible.
focus: Calculate shear displacement Δx = FL/(AG)
Calculate fractional volume change ΔV/V = p/B
Compare compressibility of solids, liquids and gases
remember: G = FL/(AΔx); G ≈ Y/3
B = −p/(ΔV/V); compressibility k = 1/B
B: solids > liquids > gases
Water B ≈ 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa; glass ≈ 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Pa
traps: Gases have the smallest bulk modulus, not the largest
The minus sign in B is there because volume decreases when pressure increases

learn.hook: Stretch a rubber band and watch it get thinner. That sideways shrinking, compared with the stretch, is Poisson's ratio.
points: When a wire is stretched, it also gets thinner. Lateral strain = Δd/d; longitudinal strain = ΔL/L.
Poisson's ratio = lateral strain/longitudinal strain (magnitudes). It has no units or dimensions; for steel it is about 0.28–0.30.
Work done in stretching a wire is stored as elastic potential energy: U = ½ × stress × strain × volume = ½ F ΔL.
Energy density (per unit volume): u = ½ × stress × strain = ½ Y (strain)² = (stress)²/(2Y).

example.q: A wire stretched by 2 mm under a final load of 100 N. Find the elastic energy stored.
steps: U = ½ F ΔL.

learn.reallife: Catapult (gulel) users in villages store elastic energy in stretched rubber; the energy is ½ × stress × strain × volume of the rubber.

items.q: Load and stretch both doubled: U × ?

quiz.q: A wire of length 1 m and diameter 1 mm is stretched by 1 mm, and its diameter decreases by 0.0003 mm. Poisson's ratio is
quiz.explain: Lateral strain = 0.0003/1 = 3 × 10⁻⁴; longitudinal = 1/1000 = 10⁻³; ratio = 0.3.
steps: Lateral strain = 0.0003 mm/1 mm = 3 × 10⁻⁴
Longitudinal strain = 1 mm/1000 mm = 10⁻³
Poisson's ratio = 3 × 10⁻⁴/10⁻³ = 0.3
Answer: 0.3

quiz.q: Poisson's ratio has
quiz.explain: It is a ratio of two strains.
steps: Poisson's ratio = lateral strain/longitudinal strain.
A ratio of two strains has no units.
Answer: No units or dimensions
quiz.mistake: Thinks it has the unit of stress

quiz.q: The elastic potential energy per unit volume of a stretched wire is
quiz.explain: u = ½ × stress × strain.
steps: Stored energy U = ½ × stress × strain × volume.
Divide by volume: energy per volume = ½ × stress × strain.
Answer: ½ × stress × strain

quiz.q: A wire stretched by 4 mm under 500 N stores energy (in J)
steps: U = ½FΔL, ΔL = 4 mm = 0.004 m
U = 1 J
Answer: 1
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ or the unit conversion

quiz.q: A wire of volume 10⁻⁶ m³ has stress 2 × 10⁸ Pa and strain 10⁻³. The stored elastic energy in J is
steps: U = ½ × stress × strain × volume
Answer: 0.1

quiz.q: When a wire is stretched, its diameter
quiz.explain: Lateral contraction accompanies longitudinal extension.
steps: A stretched wire gets longer and thinner (lateral contraction).
So its diameter decreases.
Answer: Decreases
quiz.mistake: Thinks volume must grow in every direction

quiz.q: Energy density in a stretched wire can also be written as
quiz.explain: u = ½ stress × strain and stress = Y × strain.
steps: u = ½ × stress × strain, and stress = Y × strain.
u = ½ × Y × strain × strain
u = ½ Y (strain)²
Answer: ½ Y (strain)²

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Work done in stretching a wire is stored as elastic potential energy.
Reason (R): The restoring force is conservative within the elastic limit, so the work can be recovered.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Within the elastic limit, the wire gives back the energy on release. R explains A.
steps: R: within the elastic limit the restoring force is conservative, so the work can be recovered: true.
So the work is stored as elastic PE: A true.
R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the work is all lost as heat

teach.ask: Gappu stretched a rubber vine to launch a seed and noticed it got thinner. Explain Poisson's ratio and the energy stored in a stretched wire.
teach.praise: Thinner as it gets longer: Poisson's ratio! And the energy stored is ½ × stress × strain × volume.
teach.nudge: How do you compare the thinning with the stretching? How much energy does a stretched wire store?

revise.summary: A stretched wire also gets thinner; Poisson's ratio = lateral strain/longitudinal strain, with no units (≈ 0.28–0.30 for steel). Work done in stretching is stored as elastic energy U = ½FΔL, with energy density ½ × stress × strain = ½Y(strain)².
focus: Calculate Poisson's ratio
Calculate stored elastic energy ½FΔL
Use energy density ½ × stress × strain
remember: Poisson's ratio = (Δd/d)/(ΔL/L), no units
U = ½FΔL = ½ × stress × strain × volume
u = ½ × stress × strain = ½Y(strain)² = (stress)²/(2Y)
traps: Don't forget the ½ in the energy formula
Stretching a wire makes its diameter smaller, not larger

learn.hook: Why are bridge girders shaped like the letter I, and why can't mountains on Earth be much taller than about 10 km? Elasticity answers both.
points: Crane ropes: the rope's area must keep stress below the yield strength, with a safety factor (say 10). Ropes are made of many thin wires twisted together for flexibility and strength.

Beams: sag of a beam (length l, breadth b, depth d) loaded at the middle: δ = Wl³/(4bd³Y). Increasing depth d reduces sag greatly (d³), so beams are deep; an I-section saves material and resists buckling.
Pillars with distributed (bevelled) ends carry more load than those with rounded ends.
Mountains: the rock at the base would flow under shear stress if a mountain were much taller than about 10 km on Earth.
Typical numericals: elongations with Y, shear displacements with G, volume changes with B, and ratios of elongations for different wires.

example.q: A crane must lift 10⁴ kg. The rope's yield strength is 3 × 10⁸ Pa (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the minimum cross-sectional area, and with a safety factor of 10.
steps: Load = mg = 10⁵ N.
With safety factor 10: A ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻³ m² (radius about 3 cm).

learn.reallife: The I-shaped steel girders used in Delhi Metro's elevated viaducts are chosen to resist bending with minimum steel.

games.title: Application ↔ elastic idea
pairs: Stress below yield strength with safety factor
Many thin wires in a rope
Shear limit of rock at the base

quiz.q: For a beam loaded at its centre, the sag is δ = Wl³/(4bd³Y). If the depth d is doubled, the sag becomes how many times?
steps: δ ∝ 1/d³
d → 2d: δ_new/δ = 1/2³
Answer: 1/8

quiz.q: Why are girders often given an I-shaped cross-section?
options: It gives large depth for bending resistance with less material and prevents buckling
It reduces their weight to zero
It makes them lighter only for transport
quiz.explain: Most bending resistance comes from material far from the centre; the I-shape puts it there.
steps: Bending resistance comes mainly from material far from the centre.
An I-section puts material there: large depth with less material.
It also resists buckling.
Answer: It gives large depth for bending resistance with less material and prevents buckling
quiz.mistake: Thinks the shape changes the material's Y

quiz.q: A crane rope must lift 6 × 10⁴ N. If the yield strength is 3 × 10⁸ Pa, the minimum area (no safety factor) in units of 10⁻⁴ m² is
steps: A = F/σ_y
In units of 10⁻⁴ m²: 2
Answer: 2

quiz.q: Why is a crane rope made of many thin wires twisted together rather than one thick wire?
options: To increase its yield strength tenfold
Because thick wires cannot carry tension
To reduce its Young's modulus to zero
For flexibility and ease of manufacture, with similar strength
quiz.explain: Thin strands bend easily while together giving the required area.
steps: One thick wire would be stiff and hard to bend and make.
Many thin wires twisted together bend easily.
Together they give the same area and similar strength.
Answer: For flexibility and ease of manufacture, with similar strength
quiz.mistake: Thinks twisting changes the material properties

quiz.q: The maximum height of a mountain on Earth (about 10 km) is limited by
options: The shear (elastic) strength of rock at its base
quiz.explain: Too tall a mountain would make the base rock flow under stress.
steps: A very tall mountain puts huge shear stress on the rock at its base.
Beyond about 10 km the rock would flow.
So the limit is set by the elastic (shear) strength of the base rock.
Answer: The shear (elastic) strength of rock at its base

quiz.q: Two wires A and B of the same length carry the same load. Y_A = 2Y_B and r_A = 2r_B. Ratio of elongations ΔL_A/ΔL_B is
steps: ΔL = FL/(AY) ∝ 1/(r²Y) (same F, L)
Answer: 1/8

quiz.q: A steel wire of length 4 m and area 2 × 10⁻⁶ m² stretches 2 mm under a load (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa). The load in N is
steps: F = YAΔL/L
Answer: 200

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Pillars with distributed (bevelled) ends support more load than pillars with rounded ends.
Reason (R): Distributing the load over a larger contact area reduces stress at the ends.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Smaller stress at the ends lets the pillar carry more load safely. R explains A.
steps: R: spreading the load over more area lowers stress at the ends: true.
Lower stress lets the pillar carry more load: A true.
R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the shape of ends doesn't matter

teach.ask: Gappu wants to build a twig bridge that doesn't sag. Explain how elasticity guides beam shapes, rope design and even mountain heights.
teach.praise: Make the beam deep (sag ∝ 1/d³), use I-shapes, keep ropes below yield stress, and mountains max out near 10 km!
teach.nudge: Which dimension of a beam reduces sag the most? How do engineers make sure a rope won't fail?

revise.summary: Elastic ideas guide design: crane ropes keep stress below yield strength with a safety factor, beams are made deep because sag δ = Wl³/(4bd³Y) falls as d³, and bevelled pillars carry more load. Rock strength limits Earth's mountains to about 10 km.
focus: Find minimum rope area from yield strength
Use δ ∝ 1/d³ for beam sag and explain I-sections
Compare elongations of different wires
remember: Rope area A = F/σ_y (× safety factor)
Beam sag δ = Wl³/(4bd³Y)
ΔL ∝ L/(r²Y)
traps: Doubling the beam depth reduces sag 8 times, not 2 times
Twisting thin wires is for flexibility, not to raise yield strength
